newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: MOZAMBICAN GAS PROJECT SEEN ONSTREAM BY 2000.
newsitem.headline: MOZAMBICAN GAS PROJECT SEEN ONSTREAM BY 2000.

text.p: Mozambique's Pande gas field project may be onstream by 2000, providing a number of trade and fiscal changes were made, Tony Way, senior vice president of Enron Development Corp said on Friday.

Despite already having the support of the Mozambican and South African governments, changes in taxation laws on both sides of the border were needed before gas produced could be viably transported from Mozambique to South Africa, he said.
Speaking at the Africa Upstream 1996 conference, Way said that an agreement on equal cross-border trade treatment also needed to be reached.
"Having said that we are confident that by the end of next year we will have completed the development and will be onstream by the year 2000," Way said.

The Pande gas field holds recoverable reserves of 2.5 trillion cubic feet and will find its main commercial market in South Africa. Gas will be transported from the field via Maputo to South Africa by means of a 900 km pipeline.

It is being developed by Enron together with state-owned ENH-Hidrocarbonetos De Mocambique. Sales are being negotiated with South Africa's Industrial Development Corp for possible use at an iron ore reduction plant in Mpumalanga province.

The pipeline would be expandable to accomodate incremental gas flows and ENH exploration director Guilhermino Fortes said both ENH and Enron were "keen to talk to companies interested in incremental gas sales".
"The success of the Pande project is integral to the future of the petroleum industry in Mozambique," Fortes told business and government delegates from around the world.

Pande's success was dependent on balancing Mozambique and foreign investor interests, continued donor aid and creating a pipeline infrastructure for further upstream development with offtake points in Mozambique and South Africa, he said.
Pande's development could make several other prospective areas and smaller fields economically viable, Fortes said.
ENH was seeking to license additional exploration acreage both onshore and offshore Mozambique and several foreign companies were currently in negotiations with ENH.
Fortes said that although no oil had yet been discovered in Mozambique, the potential for such discoveries existed.

"Mozambique contains substantial reserves of natural gas. No oil has been discovered to date but potential for finding oil exists. Moxambique has large sedimentary basons which are are relatively unexplored," he said.
